implementation_notes: Java's intrinsic locking is the pattern in its purest form: the compiler emits the monitorenter/monitorexit pair around a synchronized block or method, so release is bound to the block structure and an exception cannot leak the lock; the thread cannot be made to forget it. The explicit form - Lock.lock() with unlock() in a finally, exactly as the Lock javadoc prescribes - is needed only for timed or interruptible acquisition, fairness, non-block-structured locking or several condition variables. Synchronize on a dedicated private object rather than on this.
pitfalls: Synchronizing on this, on a Class object or on an interned string exposes the monitor to unrelated code; use a private final lock object.
Intrinsic locks cannot time out, be interrupted, or be released before the block ends, so I/O inside a synchronized block serializes the whole application with no escape hatch.

Blocking inside a synchronized block pins the carrier thread on virtual-thread JDKs before JEP 491 (JDK 24); on older JDKs prefer java.util.concurrent locks in code that blocks inside critical sections.

variants.name: declarative transaction demarcation (@Transactional / container-managed transactions)
variants.idiom_name: @Transactional service methods intercepted by a transaction manager
variants.implementation_notes: The enterprise realization: a proxy or interceptor around the service method starts the transaction, and with it the database locks and the ORM session's version checks, so business code contains no begin, commit or lock call; propagation, isolation, read-only and rollback rules are declarative configuration on the annotation or the deployment descriptor. This is PoEAA's Implicit Lock at the service layer, with the essential caveat that proxy-based interception reaches only calls that pass through the proxy. Programmatic transactions (PlatformTransactionManager, UserTransaction) stay justified when the transaction boundary is only known at runtime.
pitfalls: Proxy interception does not apply to self-invocation (this.other()) or to objects built outside the container: the transaction silently does not exist, so locking silently does not happen.

The default rollback rule covers unchecked exceptions only; checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor is configured, and readOnly=true permits the provider to skip locks the caller assumed were taken.
Remote calls or user interactions inside an intercepted method hold the transaction and its locks for the whole call; timeout aborts the transaction but does not release locks earlier.
